title: Fatty George's jazz house, ten-day festival and the Austrian trombonist
summary: Fatty George's Vienna club had life-size photos of Bix, Bunk and the Eureka Band. The Straws played there nightly, toured afterward, recorded two tapes, and picked up trombonist William Mirwald.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well, that was about the only ones that were there at the time. You see, I don't know, I guess it's sort of traditional. This house of jazz, any time a famous musician or a celebrity passes through, they should stop in this place and sign the book. So, it just so happens that we were in there when these people, Pettiford and Ella came through. And, you know, being in a place like that, you just get to see all the celebrities, all the greats and whatnot. Incidentally, this fellow that ran the place, his name was Fatty George. He's an Austrian. And he really goes for the old New Orleans jazz. I mean, that's the only kind of music he really took an interest in, you see. And on the walls in his place, he's got life-size pictures of Baiderbeck playing with, I think it was Tommy Darcy. On another wall, he's got Bum Johnson and a group that he was playing with. And on another wall, he's got the Eureka Brass Band. I mean, the wall is just covered with these life-size pictures, you see. And so many of the people over there, you know, the people that really went to his place, that like jazz, they've heard of New Orleans. But to them, it was more of a legendary place. They never actually thought they'd get to see people and hear people directly from New Orleans playing music over there, see. So, we played and we made a week, I always say over that week. So, Fatty had pictures made of our group. Of course, not life-size, but they were very big pictures and he put them on the wall next to all the greats, you see. And, I mean, you know, it kind of does something for you. It makes you feel like you're somebody, you know. And, well, the people over there were autograph hounds. They went for autograph. I must have signed my name about 50 times while I was over there. You know, little things like that that make you feel good about playing, you know. All I know, we really, really had a fine. You see, well, ten days we stayed at this festival. Now, we were playing, oh, maybe three, maybe four times a day during the festival, see. Every time they'd have a rally going over here, they'd call a band. And they might have one over here, they'd call a band again. So, we would, you know, we were keeping pretty active. Plus, our little job we had in town every night, see, when we were playing over at Fatty's. So, well, like I say, the festival lasted ten days. And after the ten days were up, well, we sort of took off on more or less a vacation. See, we went on our own then. John Chaff went to Paris. Bill and Carol Lee went to Munich. They stayed over at Carol's brother's house. And Bob Ice, and myself, and JJ. I'm at a loss for his last name right now. Joyce. JJ Joyce. We went to Salzburg. And we went to this little mountain resort, the Zolom Z, they call it. And we lived it up there. We had quite a time. You playing? No. Well, as a matter of fact, we left our instruments in Vienna. We left them in Vienna. And on the way back through, we picked them up. And, well, when we went back to pick these instruments up, we made two tapes in Fatty's place. You know, during the, oh, it must have been midday. Nobody was in the place. And, you know, the tape itself had good effect. It didn't have any background noise and whatnot. And if I'm not mistaken, I think Bob Ice might have this tape. And to my way of thinking, I don't know, they might have a different opinion on it, but I think that was as good as our group ever sound. You know, all the while we won this trip, see. And it was terrific. I wish I could come by this tape one day. I'd like to just listen to the stuff again, you know. What did Bill Lee play? Bill played clarinet. Well, he's clarinet and sax, man. But on this Vienna trip, he played strictly clarinet. Briss Jones didn't make the trip, see. Bill's wife played piano, because Della Husa couldn't make the trip. I think he was on duty with the National Guard at the time. So, Carol Lee played piano. Bill Lee played the clarinet. I played cornet. John played the banjo. J.J. played the drums. Ice played bass. And we picked up a trombone player while we were over there. A fellow by the name of William Mirwald. He's an Austrian. And, well, you'd swear this guy was born in New Orleans, Austria. He could play a tailgate trombone. It was out of this world, you know. And he promised to come over here. He wanted to come to New Orleans and get back with the group. And, of course, he must have thought we were playing full time, you see. I mean, he couldn't quite make a living out of something like that, you know, just off and on.
You don't know how to spell that name, huh?
I think it is M-E-E-R-V-A-L-D. I think that's the way he spelled it. William Mirwald.

Bob Ice should have it. Yeah, I think he has his address and all, you know. He's gonna keep contact with him. Incidentally, John enrolled Willie as a correspondent member in New Orleans Jazz Club, you know. So that's one more finger reaching out across the sea, you know. So Willie's a member now, I think.
